author: saden1
body:
`#2046` fixed one instance of a defect class; this sweeps the class, regenerates four committed PDFs that were describing a layout the engine no longer produces, and fixes the reason nobody noticed the fourth of them.

## Problem / Why

**The shear.** `.cell-stage` (`lib/forms/cell/stage/stage.css`) is a bounded clipping cell — `flex: 1 1 auto; min-height: 0; overflow: clip`. Every direct child of it is therefore a flex ITEM, and a flex item's default `min-height: auto` is a CONTENT-height floor. A component body that does not say `min-height: 0` refuses to shrink into the cell that clips it, so the box grows past the stage and the clip takes whatever chrome sits between the last line of text and the box's own bottom edge: the bottom border, the radii, the bottom of a filled panel. Every word is still readable, and the export then tags the slide "Content clipped" — true of the box, false of the text.

**The head loss, which is worse.** A box that centers and then overflows splits the excess evenly, so half of it goes off the BLOCK-START edge — and block-start overflow does not grow `scrollHeight`, so nothing in this system can see it. A cut tail announces itself; a cut head does not. `stage.css` has required `safe` alignment since #1299, but several components set their own bare `center` and were losing real text off the top of slides that looked fine.

**The stale PDFs, and the detector that hid one.** A committed PDF that no longer matches the engine makes every future `npm run preview` diff on that deck lie, which is how a real regression gets waved through. Four were stale — and the tool that reports "what visually changed" was silently scoring the single worst page of them zero (§4).

## What changed

### 1 · `examples/gallery-jargon.pdf` regenerated

Five of its 58 pages showed a layout the engine no longer produces. Attribution, by rendering the deck in a worktree at each commit and comparing page-by-page with `compare -metric AE`:

| render | differing pages vs the committed PDF |
|---|---|
| `3ce461b` (the commit before #2011) | **0 of 58** |
| `e30e5fe` — `feat(cards)!` (#2011) | 5 — pages 10, 11, 12, 17, 25 |
| `HEAD` | the same 5, pixel-identical to #2011's render |

So #2011 left it behind and it is the only one; #2030, #2013, #2043, #2046 and #2037 all render this deck identically. All five pages are card grids (`cards-grid` ×4, `verdict-grid` ×1) — the two components #2011 rewrote. Under the new `cards:` register a card row shrink-wraps and centers instead of stretching, so the old PDF showed cards with large empty interiors.

Rendering is deterministic here (two consecutive renders diff to 0 on all 58 pages), and a from-scratch rebuild of the regenerated file diffs to 0 against it on all 58.

> **The `golden-diff` bot comment is the receipt for §4.** On the first head it reported **4** changed slides for this deck against the 5 stated here; on the head carrying §4 it reports **5**, with every other golden's count unchanged. That was not a tolerance difference — page 17 differs by 1,159,660px, which `compare` prints as `1.15966e+06`, which the parse rejected and scored **0**.

### 2 · Ten declarations across eight components

A static pass over all 86 files in `lib/components/**`, `lib/base/**` and `lib/forms/**` found 109 growing-flex declarations, 79 with no `min-height: 0` plausibly applying. A dynamic pass read the COMPUTED style of every direct stage child across the 84 staged sections of the CI baseline gallery in a real Chromium and found 20 with a growing flex and `min-height: auto`. Every direct stage child from either list was then pressed with a hand-authored dense fixture and an overstuffed control at `size: hd` — 16:9 is the shortest landscape stage and `hd` is the default, so it is where the shear bites first. It is aspect ratio, not resolution.

| component | measured before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `compare-prose` — the card row | 445.06px in a 438.22px stage, 6.84px shorn off both cards, ink 14.34px inside | no hang, ink unmoved |
| `decision` — the option row | 412.88px in a 393.44px stage, 19.44px shorn incl. the 3px `--decision-accent` border | no hang |
| `redline` — the plain clause only | 429.28px against a 406.28px share, 23.00px of border, radius and left rail shorn | no hang |
| `matrix-2x2` — the quadrant list | 448.78px in a 438.22px stage, both bottom quadrants 10.56px out | no hang |
| `statute-stack` — the three rails | 446.63px in a 438.22px stage, ALL THREE rails 8.41px out | no hang |
| `policy-recommendation` — the rationale list | held 282.56px against a 276.12px share, pushed the ask bar 6.44px out | no hang |
| `citation-card.pull-quote` — the hero quote | 294px where the stage could give it 249.50px, pushed the gloss 44.50px out — here the clip was into TEXT, 15.17px of the gloss outside | no hang, ink 29.33px inside |
| `citation-card.split` — both centerings | the gloss sat 25.02px ABOVE the stage top, **21.02px of text gone** | nothing above the top edge |
| `cycle` — the ring, and the stage's centering | 471.94px ring in a 400.44px stage, 35.75px off EACH edge, **16.75px of text gone off the top**, return arc and ↻ mark entirely below the clip | ring exactly stage height, arc and mark back |
| `statute-stack.preemption` — its centering | **self-inflicted; caught by checker #1.** Releasing the base list's floor let `.preemption`'s bare `center` split the excess both ways: 53.53px of real text above the stage top on a four-card stack, 129.56px on a five-card one, taking the FEDERAL label, its citation pill and the card's top border off the slide. Unclamped, the same deck put all 125.97px of its loss out the bottom, visibly | nothing above the top edge; the rail chrome the base fix bought is kept |

**"Chrome only" holds for six of the nine shear cases, not all nine** — on `pull-quote`, `split` and `cycle` the fixture loses words too, so the fix recovers text as well as chrome. author: stevevanhooser
body:
Closes #151.

MATLAB sets `resp.ind = ind_real` (`tuning_response.m:834`) — the **raw** individual responses. The Python port returned the control-subtracted ones instead. `blankind` already matched; only `ind` differed.

## Why the distinction is not cosmetic

These values can be complex. An F1 or F2 response carries a phase that depends on when the stimulus happened to start — this module's own docstring says so — and the control is measured in a different window, so the relative phase between a response and its control is arbitrary.

Complex subtraction is vector subtraction, so that arbitrary phase moves the answer. Signal magnitude 10, control magnitude 3:

| relative phase | `abs(a - b)` |
|---|---|
| 0° | 7.00 |
| 90° | 10.44 |
| 180° | 13.00 |

`abs(a) - abs(b)` is **7.00 throughout** — an 86% swing driven purely by a quantity that isn't comparable in the first place. On a whole curve it doesn't merely add noise: with random control phases a suppression of −0.91 came out as a response of 4.67.

**Nothing needed the difference.** The control individuals are returned alongside as `blankind`, and recorded per point in the `stimulus_tuningcurve` document, so a caller comparing the two groups — which is what `neural_response_significance` does — compares magnitudes, and that is well defined.

`curve` is still built from the subtracted means, as in MATLAB: a tuning curve is about response above baseline, and its mean is taken before the magnitude is. The two coexist in one struct on purpose.

## The index path is left alone

MATLAB's `oridirtuning.m:151` does complex-subtract for the vector and fit indices, and this does not change that. The same phase argument reaches it, but whether those indices should use `abs(a) - abs(b)` is a question about the analysis rather than the port, and it would move published numbers. It stays recorded in #151 for a decision by someone who knows the science; parity with MATLAB is kept meanwhile.

## Tests

Three, all of which fail against the previous behaviour:

- `ind` holds the raw individuals
- `ind` and `curve` deliberately answer different questions
- a complex response is not subtracted before its magnitude is taken

The absence of any assertion on `ind` is what let this ship — the existing tests covered `curve`, `blankresp`, `spont` and `spontind`, never `ind`.

## Also fixed: a stale docstring I shipped

`ndi.app.oridirtuning`'s module docstring still announced the index half as *"NOT implemented, and deliberately not worked around"* — which stopped being true in the same PR that implemented it (#145). I updated the code and not the prose above it. Rewritten to say where the math actually comes from and why two response structs exist.

The comment in `calculate_oridir_indexes` explaining why it doesn't call this helper is updated too: the reason is no longer that the helper disagrees with MATLAB, but that the index call needs the subtracted individuals the helper doesn't return — so the loop has to exist regardless, and calling the helper as well would compute everything twice.

`response_individual` in the helper became dead once `ind` stopped using it, and is removed.

## Verification

- Full suite — 3715 passed, 225 skipped
- Symmetry — 53 passed, only the pre-existing tgz fixture failure
- `ruff` and `black` clean

Five ontology failures (`test_ontology_reexport.py` collection, four in `test_ontology_lookup_call_sites.py`) are **pre-existing on clean main** — verified by stashing this branch's changes and re-running. They need an `ndi_ontology` package not installed in my environment, and are unrelated to this change.

count is corrected and the parenthetical dropped. `skills/incident-drill/` also still existed on
disk as an untracked directory holding nothing but `scripts/__pycache__/*.pyc` from the deleted
skill, which made `ls -d skills/*/ | wc -l` report 29 against 28 `SKILL.md` files and so made
README's corrected "28 skills" read as wrong to anyone who checked it the obvious way. It is

author: ghajaymore
body:
D5 of the 2026-09-02 exploratory audit, and the arithmetic is worth writing down because it is not obvious from either half on its own.

`finishOrderFor` carried unranked players into `pointsForRank` with a rank of 0. That function is 1-BASED: `table[rank - 1]` reads `table[-1]`, which is undefined and contributes nothing — and then the loop walks FORWARD into `table[0]`, the winner's points. With the default table of 100, 80, 65, 55, three non-returners sharing rank 0 scored

    (table[-1] + table[0] + table[1]) / 3  =  (0 + 100 + 80) / 3  =  60

each, above the player who actually finished fourth on fifty-five. A twenty-player hand-scored event — a round the app explicitly does not rank — handed all twenty members 34.7 points on the same walk.

FIXED IN BOTH PLACES, and they fix different things.

At the source, `finishOrderFor` now reports only players who returned something. That is the real fix, and it is the only one that addresses the quieter half: each rank-0 entry also incremented `played`, which is what `minEvents` counts, so somebody who never teed up could qualify for the order of merit on absences alone. `positionsFrom` already applied exactly this filter; this function was written without it.

Match play needed it too, and for a different reason: `overall` numbers everybody `i + 1`, so a player who took no part still occupied a finishing position. The filter runs BEFORE the index, which is what makes the survivors re-rank 1..N contiguously — filtering afterwards would leave them ranked 1, 3, 4 with a hole where the absentee was, and those gaps are read straight off the points table.

At the sink, `pointsForRank` refuses any rank below 1. The source fix means nothing should arrive there, but the function is exported, 1-based, and nothing in its signature says so — so a future caller gets the safe answer rather than the winner's points.

Mutation checked: removing the sink guard reproduces SIXTY, which is the number the audit reported, arrived at independently here.

The source filter is pinned by reading `series.ts` rather than by behaviour. The honest reason is that producing one unranked row through `loadEventState` needs a whole event — players, cards, standings — and the arithmetic that actually decides the points is tested properly above. What the source assertions add is the one line that decides WHO is handed to it, both branches, and the ordering of filter before index.

Closes #38. Linear BAS-49.

The taker exam (#32) showed every per-game model loses on Kalshi after crossing the spread and paying the taker fee. This PR asks the next question from `docs/money-exam-2026.md`: what if we post limit orders at fair value minus a margin and let the market come to us?

## What was built

- **Candle archive.** `scripts/backfill_kalshi_candles.py` pulls Kalshi hourly candlesticks for every 2026 KXMLBGAME market from T−24h to first pitch, checkpointed every 50 markets, retrying through 429s. 876/876 markets, 20,989 candles, 0.27 MB, committed at `data/market/kalshi_candles_2026.parquet`. Integrity: the archive's last pre-pitch candle reproduces the independently built closes parquet (price, bid, ask, timestamp) on 875/876 markets.
- **Maker mode in `src/market/pnl.py`.** Post at `P_model − m` on the YES side (mirror for NO), live T−24h → first pitch, one contract per game, cancel at pitch. Fill rule: first hourly candle whose low ≤ q with volume > 0. Maker fee `0.0175·C·P·(1−P)` (a quarter of the taker rate, 0.44¢ max; exposed as `--kalshi-maker-fee-rate`; `--maker-round-cents` prices the harsher per-cent rounding). Margin chosen on the first half of the window by date, scored on the second. Shuffled-edge control, bootstrap CI, flat and quarter-Kelly. `scripts/money_exam.py --maker --markdown` prints the grid.

## Result — test half (377 games, 2026-08-05 → 09-02, flat)

| Model | m | fill | ¢/posted | ROI | 95% CI |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| pythag_60_sp_lu_bp | 0.00 | 1.000 | −7.79¢ | −15.7% | (−26.0, −5.6) |
| | 0.02 | 0.828 | −5.15¢ | −12.9% | (−24.8, −1.4) |
| | **0.05** (chosen) | 0.377 | **−0.54¢** | **−3.1%** | (−21.7, +15.2) |
| …shuffled control | 0.05 | 0.430 | −1.16¢ | −5.2% | (−19.8, +9.2) |
| pythag_60 | 0.05 | 0.562 | −3.66¢ | −14.5% | (−28.7, +0.4) |
| home_constant | 0.05 | 0.735 | −3.39¢ | −10.3% | (−23.4, +2.8) |

**Crossing vs quoting on the same 377 games:** stack −10.9% (taker) → −3.1% (maker). 7.8 points recovered, against the 8.4 the taker decomposition blamed on spread (4.0) + fee (4.4). And −3.1% is where the taker exam's *frictionless* row already put this book (−3.2%): two instruments built from different data agree on the decomposition to a tenth of a point.

**Reading.** No real model has a positive cell anywhere in the 50-row grid; three of four shuffled controls beat their model; fills land at 45%. Costs were the difference between losing 11 points and losing 3. There is no edge underneath either. The doc says so, and the station M money row of `docs/architecture.md` now reads the same way. Routes that remain: props (BAS-46, in flight), and a per-game model that actually beats the close on Brier (station E residual .0027, t≈2).

## Tests

+33 (fill at the low, no fill above the bid, no fill on zero volume, NO-side mirror, cancel at first pitch, no fill before posting, the leakage guard, the marketable flag, archive resume / skip-one-bad-market). Suite **460 passed**. Taker tables and the Brier table reproduce the doc's existing numbers exactly.

## Reproduce

```
python scripts/backfill_kalshi_candles.py --season 2026
python scripts/money_exam.py --markdown            # taker
python scripts/money_exam.py --maker --markdown    # maker

author: somtri
body:
Fixes #126135.

## Problem

`RaggedGather` with int32 `Tsplits` can compute a total output value count that exceeds int32. The count is accumulated in the splits type (`ragged_gather_op.cc`), so it wraps. The wrapped, smaller count is used to allocate the output values tensor, but the copy loop still walks the full un-wrapped set of slices, so it writes past the allocation. AddressSanitizer reports a heap-buffer-overflow write at `ragged_gather_op.cc:47`.

Repro from the issue:

```python
tf.raw_ops.RaggedGather(
    params_nested_splits=[tf.constant([0, 65536], tf.int32)],
    params_dense_values=tf.zeros([65536], tf.uint8),
    indices=tf.zeros([65537], tf.int32),
    OUTPUT_RAGGED_RANK=1,
)
```

The true count is `65537 * 65536 = 2**32 + 65536`, which wraps to `65536` in int32.

## Fix

Accumulate the value count in `int64_t`, then validate it against `std::numeric_limits<SPLITS_TYPE>::max()` before the output is allocated, returning `InvalidArgumentError` on overflow. This follows the existing guard in `ragged_range_op.cc` ("Number of rows exceeds limits of Tsplits"). Valid inputs are unaffected: the narrowed count equals the previous value.

## Test

Adds `testValueCountOverflowError` to `ragged_gather_op_test.py`. It drives the raw `RaggedGather` op to pin `Tsplits=int32`, because the high-level `ragged_gather_ops.gather` defaults to int64 splits and cannot reproduce the wrap. The test inputs are small: the guard returns the error before the oversized output is allocated, so the test does not need gigabytes of memory.

## Out of scope

The kernel keeps several `int`-typed index locals (`out_pos` in `WriteValueSlices`, and `start`, `limit`, and the loop counters in `MakeSplits`). This guard caps the value count at the `Tsplits` maximum, so for int32 `Tsplits` those locals cannot overflow. They stay a pre-existing truncation only for int64 `Tsplits` gathering more than `INT_MAX` values, which needs a multi-gigabyte output. That is a separate issue and is not changed here.

## Verification

I did not build locally. Runtime verification is left to the TensorFlow presubmit CI, which builds and runs `ragged_gather_op_test`.

author: artjack
body:
**VERDICT-F-43**, run 9's sharpest finding, and the only one of its seven whose cure is a prompt change rather than code.

### The trap

The contract tells the tester to prove causation by flipping the suspected cause in a scratch copy of the tree. The bash guard was widened in 0.65.0 specifically so `cp -a <checkout> <scratch>` would be permitted — for exactly this purpose.

A copied tree carries the project's virtualenv. An editable install's `.pth` names the **original** checkout absolutely, and site-packages wins unless something is put ahead of it. So the scratch imports the unmodified source, and every injection reads as a no-op.

Verdict measured it rather than reasoning about it — four defects injected into a scratch copy, each run twice, identical but for one environment variable:

| | defects caught |
|---|---|
| without `PYTHONPATH` | **0 of 4** |
| with `PYTHONPATH=<scratch>/src` | **4 of 4** |

### Why it is not a footnote

A false negative here reads as a green counterfactual. The contract converts that into `fix_verified: true`. `_stamp_outcome` converts *that* into a `confirmed` ledger row. The published track record counts it as "held up".

Silent, and self-flattering in precisely the direction those calibration rules exist to prevent. The finding also stated plainly what it could not establish — whether runs 5 through 8 fell into the same trap — because the state records a re-injection's result and never its command.

### The fix

§3 now carries the isolation step, the one-line check to run before trusting a result (`python -c "import <pkg>; print(<pkg>.__file__)"` must print a path inside the scratch), and the flat statement that a green counterfactual you did not isolate is evidence of nothing. §6's `fix_verified` clause points at it.

The harness's own verifier has always done this and records the `pythonpath` it used. Only the agent-facing prose was missing it — the machine side knew what the contract did not say.

### The eval was paid

Prompt edits are eval-paid in this project. The seeded pricer eval scores **6/6 with no hard failures** against the edited prompt, matching the published baseline.

A documentation-shaped change to a prompt is still a behaviour change, and the only way to know it did not regress is to run the thing. 690 tests unchanged.

### gRPC-Go: xDS RBAC and HTTP/2 Vulnerabilities
[GHSA-hrxh-6v49-42gf](https://redirect.github.com/advisories/GHSA-hrxh-6v49-42gf)

<details>
<summary>More information</summary>

#### Details
Multiple security vulnerabilities have been identified and addressed in grpc-go affecting the xDS RBAC authorization engine (internal/xds/rbac) and the HTTP/2 transport server implementation (internal/transport). These vulnerabilities could result in:

- Authorization Bypass (Fail-Open) when translating xDS RBAC policies containing `Metadata` or `RequestedServerName` fields.
- Denial of Service (High CPU Consumption) due to an HTTP/2 Rapid Reset mitigation bypass during client-initiated stream resets.
- Denial of Service (Server Panic) when parsing crafted xDS RBAC policies containing `NOT` rules around unsupported fields.

##### Impact
_What kind of vulnerability is it? Who is impacted?_

##### xDS RBAC Authorization Bypass via `Metadata` & `RequestedServerName` matchers

- Affected Component: xDS RBAC 
- Impact: When building policy matchers for gRPC RBAC from xDS configurations, unsupported `permission` and `principal` rules (specifically `Metadata` and `RequestedServerName`) were silently ignored and treated as no-ops.
  - If an authorization policy relied purely on these matchers for access control, treating those rules as no-ops effectively removed the restrictions.
- If these unsupported rules were nested inside logical `NOT` rules (`Permission_NotRule` / `Principal_NotId`) or multi-condition `OR/AND` rules, silently dropping them changed the boolean logic flow of the authorization engine.

As a result, policy evaluation decisions could fail open, allowing unauthorized clients to access protected gRPC services or resources.

##### HTTP/2 Rapid Reset Mitigation Bypass / Denial of Service via Stream Aborts

- Affected Component: HTTP/2 transport
- Impact: Earlier mitigations in grpc-go for HTTP/2 Rapid Reset only applied threshold checks to items that directly resulted in control frames being written back to the wire, such as `SETTINGS` ACKs or server-initiated `RST_STREAM`s.

When a client initiated a rapid flood of stream creation (`HEADERS`) immediately followed by stream termination `RST_STREAM`, items queued up in the control buffer without counting against the transport response frame threshold. An attacker can repeatedly trigger this flood sequence to bypass reader blocking, resulting in high CPU usage, and Denial of Service (DoS).

##### Denial of Service (Panic) in xDS RBAC Engine via Unsupported Fields inside NOT Rules

- Affected Component: xDS RBAC 
- Impact: The xDS RBAC policy translators recursively generate matchers for nested rules. When a `NOT` rule wrapped an unsupported or unhandled field (such as `SourcedMetadata`), the recursive step returned an empty matcher. This could result in a runtime panic when the RBAC engine attempts to authorize an incoming request.

An attacker or misconfigured/malicious xDS management server delivering an LDS/RDS update containing a `NOT` rule around an unhandled field causes the gRPC server process to crash immediately (CWE-248 / Denial of Service).

##### Patches
_Has the problem been patched? What versions should users upgrade to?_

All three issues have been fixed in `master` and will be released in 1.82.1 shortly.

##### Workarounds
_Is there a way for users to fix or remediate the vulnerability without upgrading?_

If upgrading grpc-go immediately is not possible, apply the following workarounds based on your deployment architecture:

* For xDS RBAC Vulnerabilities & Panics: Ensure that upstream xDS management servers do not push RBAC policies containing `Metadata`, `RequestedServerName`, or `NOT` rules wrapping unsupported fields (such as `SourcedMetadata`) to grpc-go servers.
* For HTTP/2 Rapid Reset DOS: Configure upstream reverse proxies or load balancers (such as Envoy) with strict HTTP/2 `max_concurrent_streams` limits and active rate limiting on `RST_STREAM` frequency per connection.

##### Severity

  | Vulnerability | Qualitative Severity | Approximate CVSS v3.1 Score | Primary Impact |
  | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
  | **xDS RBAC Authorization Bypass** | **High** | `8.2` | Unauthorized Access / Fail-Open |
  | **HTTP/2 Rapid Reset DOS Bypass** | **High** | `7.5` | High CPU Consumption / Denial of Service |
  | **xDS RBAC Engine Server Panic** | **Medium** | `5.9` | Process Crash / Denial of Service |

- CVSS Score: 8.8 / 10 (High)
- Vector String: `CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N`

### gRPC-Go: Heap Memory Exhaustion (OOM) via HTTP/2 DATA Frame Fragmentation
[CVE-2026-84304](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-84304) / [GHSA-vp52-pcj8-j9qc](https://redirect.github.com/advisories/GHSA-vp52-pcj8-j9qc)

<details>
<summary>More information</summary>

#### Details
##### Impact
An unauthenticated remote attacker can initiate a gRPC stream and purposefully fragment their payload into millions of tiny (e.g., 1-byte) HTTP/2 DATA frames. Even if the total payload volume falls within the configured connection and stream flow-control windows, each independent fragment incurs memory overhead due to internal tracking structures and queue allocation.

Repeated fragmentation massively inflates the heap space consumed by the stream. An attacker multiplexing multiple concurrent streams can exhaust the memory bounds of the runtime, forcing a runtime panic or OutOfMemory condition and leading to a remote Denial of Service (DoS).

##### Patches
The change to fix this issue is merged in `master` and a patch release, 1.83.1, has been published that contains this fix.

##### Workarounds
This vulnerability is mitigated by implementing receive buffer compaction. Consecutive small data buffers are automatically coalesced into larger buffers from a shared pool once the overhead is perceived to be excessive relative to actual payload data, drastically minimizing per-frame memory overheads.

This behavior is enabled by default. A temporary escape hatch is provided via the environment variable `GRPC_GO_EXPERIMENTAL_ENABLE_RECEIVE_BUFFER_COMPACTION=false` to disable the feature if unforeseen issues arise, but it will be removed in a future release.

Implements Phase P1 of `docs/pwa-spec.md` (ADR-0079). The reader gains an install identity — everything under `/app`, so Caddy, FastAPI and the CSP are untouched — and the two standalone-window behavior fixes. No service worker (Phase P2) and no install affordance (Phase P4).

## What's here

- **`scripts/icons.py`** (`uv run --with cairosvg`, the `scripts/fonts.py` pattern): renders `static/favicon.svg` into `frontend/public/icons/` — 192/512 `any`, 192/512 `maskable` (mark in the inner 80% on a full-bleed background; separate entries, never `"any maskable"`), opaque 180px apple-touch — writing `docs/verification/icons.json`. cairosvg ignores `textLength`, so the script measures the word's natural width (89.19 of 64 viewBox units) and applies the x0.62789 squeeze `spacingAndGlyphs` performs in a browser.
- **`frontend/public/manifest.webmanifest`** per the spec's § Manifest: `id`/`scope` `"/app/"` (trailing slash), `start_url` in scope, `standalone`, `navigate-existing`, colours read from `site.scss`'s token block (`--page` light `#f9f9f7`).
- **`Base.astro`**: manifest + apple-touch links; one `theme-color` meta defaulting light, corrected pre-paint by the theme bootstrap and moved by `ThemeToggle` on toggle; `viewport-fit=cover` paired with `env(safe-area-inset-*)` padding on `.topbar`, `.sectionbar` (in the `display: contents` band, which renders no `.topbar` box) and `.usa-footer`; the link-target script treats `matchMedia("(display-mode: standalone)").matches || navigator.standalone` as `usc-linktarget === "same"`.
- **`/app/search` and `/app/goto` carry a trail** (Home › Search), closing ADR-0065's one no-trail gap; `current` keeps an empty identifier so `PrintHeader` stays silent.
- **`frontend/tests/pwa.test.ts`** (10 tests): manifest parses; identity invariants hold; every declared icon exists at its declared pixel size via the PNG header; theme-color values in the manifest, `Base.astro` and `ThemeToggle` match the token block.
- **ADR-0079** (0077/0078 are claimed on open branches), claimed in guide chapter 02's `covers.adrs` with a two-sentence "Install as an app" stub for P4 to expand; `docs/js-budgets.json` re-measured per its headroom rule (Base's graph grew 1,268 bytes per route, all 23 ceilings move); spec Status table + BUILDLOG 096.

## Verified

- `make test-web`: **467 passed** (457 + 10 new).
- Full Playwright suite against `make dev-all` rebuilt from this branch: **661 passed, 2 skipped, 0 failed** — `sticky.spec.ts` green (`env()` is 0 in a browser; sticky geometry unmoved), a11y **343 scans, 8 violation/route pairs, 2,910 nodes**, `docs/verification/a11y.json` byte-identical to the baseline.
- `make shots`: exit 0, no horizontal overflow at 320 or 1280-at-200%; `search-*.png` show the new trail.
- Not verifiable here: an actual install (Chromium needs HTTPS, iOS has no emulation) — the manual device pass stays owed to the deploy step.
